name: CRAFT framework origin (Rishi Jain)
publisher: Rishi Jain, individual content marketer and prompting-course creator (founder of Digital Scholar, co-founder of echoVME Digital; self-described "India's most-followed AI Influencer")
date_published: Framework stated to originate in 2022, per Jain's own account on his blog (https://rrishijain.com/blog/craft-framework); exact dated primary artifact (first post, slide deck, or video) not located, only the retrospective blog post stating the 2022 origin.
source_type: practitioner framework (content-marketing mnemonic published via personal blog and paid courses)
claim_value: CRAFT is a 5-step prompt-writing mnemonic: Context (set the scene / establish who you are and your situation), Role (tell the model who to be), Action (state the task with a precise verb), Format (define the deliverable: length, structure, constraints), Tone (frame the style, ideally with a counter-example of what to avoid). Jain states he built it in 2022 after frameworks with "7 steps, 10 components, nested templates" didn't stick with his students, and designed CRAFT to be memorised and applied in 60 seconds.
claim_definition: This is a practitioner's taxonomy/mnemonic for structuring prompts, not a benchmark result or empirical finding. No controlled comparison, user study, or measured output-quality improvement is presented; the claim is pedagogical and anecdotal (what helped Jain's own students remember prompt structure), then repackaged as a general-purpose technique.
reproducibility: Not applicable in the benchmark sense: no code, dataset, or eval harness exists because no quantitative claim is being made. The only "evidence" offered is Jain's personal teaching anecdote; no independent replication of any output-quality improvement has been found.
publisher_sells_relevant_product: Yes. Jain sells prompting/AI courses that use CRAFT as teaching material and as a lead-generation hook, including the "30 Days AI Mastery Challenge," "AI Marketer Pro," a free "CRAFT Prompt Builder" tool, and corporate AI training delivered through Digital Scholar across Indian cities. CRAFT functions as branded content for these commercial offerings rather than a disinterested research contribution.
conflict_notes: CRAFT is structurally derivative of the earlier RACE framework (Role, Action, Context, Expectation), which predates it in circulation as a prompt-engineering mnemonic. The two frameworks share three of four/five core elements (Role, Action, Context) nearly verbatim; CRAFT's distinguishing moves are (1) renaming Expectation to the narrower, more concrete Format, (2) adding a fifth element, Tone, and (3) reordering Context to the front of the acronym to form a more pronounceable, brandable word (CRAFT vs. RACE). No source reviewed credits RACE or any other predecessor; Jain's own account presents CRAFT as built from scratch out of frustration with "7-step, 10-component" frameworks, with no acknowledgment of structural overlap with RACE or other contemporaneous Role/Action/Context-style mnemonics common in the prompt-engineering influencer space.
relationship: Complicates the 'prompt engineering is dead, context engineering is what matters now' framing from the opposite direction than most sources in this set: CRAFT is itself prompt-engineering content (a mnemonic for writing better prompts), produced for an audience of marketers and course buyers, not context engineering. Citing CRAFT as evidence that 'context engineering' is a mature discipline would be a category error; it is better used as an example of how much of the public prompt/context-engineering discourse is influencer content-marketing mnemonics rather than research, which is useful ammunition for distinguishing genuine engineering discipline claims from reskinned teaching acronyms.
derivative_of: Structurally derivative of RACE (Role, Action, Context, Expectation), an earlier and more widely circulated prompt-engineering mnemonic. CRAFT keeps Role, Action, and Context essentially intact, narrows Expectation into Format, adds Tone as a new fifth element, and moves Context to the front position to produce the acronym CRAFT. This is a repackaging/extension of RACE's structure under a new, more brandable name rather than an independently derived framework; no primary source locates a citation or acknowledgment of RACE by Jain.
register: practitioner/engineer (aimed at marketers, students, and general AI users learning to write prompts; not aimed at researchers or enterprise IT buyers)
notes: The 2022 origin date and the five-component definition are taken directly from Jain's own blog post (rrishijain.com/blog/craft-framework), which counts as a primary-ish source for the claim of authorship, but no independently dated artifact (a 2022 tweet, video, or slide deck) was located to verify the 2022 date itself; it rests on Jain's own retrospective account written later. The RACE-derivative relationship is based on comparing the two frameworks' published definitions side by side; no document was found where either framework's creator acknowledges the other, so the derivative-of claim is an inference from structural similarity, not a confirmed admission.
new_angle: Adds a concrete, named predecessor (RACE) that CRAFT is structurally derivative of, which sharpens the general point already logged in article_ideas.md (09-27, 'Context engineering didn't retire the prompt') that current framing vocabulary is often repackaged rather than new. This source is a clean example of a content-marketing mnemonic with explicit commercial motive (course sales, corporate training) presented as a prompting innovation, useful as a contrast case against the academic survey and vendor-blog sources already in this research set.
